newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's successful Tutsis flee witchhunt.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's successful Tutsis flee witchhunt.

text.p: Tutsis who are among some of Zaire's most successful entrepeneurs and professionals are packing up and leaving, fleeing a witchhunt after a revolt by Tutsi rebels in the east of the chaotic country.
In a late night vote on Thursday, Zaire's transitional parliament called for Tutsis to be thrown out of the army, the civil service and state-run enterprises.
Tutsi refugees arriving in neighbouring Congo all week talk of harasssment. Those left behind are growing more anxious.

"The Zaireans attacked my home and now I have to live under cover. As soon as I can I will get out to Congo," said one Tutsi on Friday. Until recently he worked as an administrator at a local factory.
Of ethnic Tutsi origin, he has lived all his life in Zaire. His family arrived from Rwanda in the 1920s.

Witnesses said a few hundred demonstrators marched to the Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo's office on Friday to demand tougher action against Tutsi-led Rwanda, which Zaire accuses of waging war in its volatile eastern refugee region.
Kinshasa's Tutsis are the latest victims of bitter Hutu-Tutsi rivalry which has poisoned life in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi for generations.

Over a million Hutu refugees have lived in camps in eastern Zaire since 1994 when they fled Rwanda fearing reprisals or an upsurge in civil war that followed the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis there.
Hundreds of Tutsis have already quit Kinshasa, most of them fleeing across the broad Zaire River into Congo.
On Monday 50 were reported to have arrived in Brazzaville, Congo's capital. Every day this week more have crossed the river, at least another 30 leaving on Thursday.
On Monday, the Tutsi chairman of cellular phone operator Telecel, Miko Rwayitare, resigned his post at the head of one of Zaire's most successful companies.
"The idea that Miko...and Telecel would be implicated in the political events that Zaire is going through today is completely absurd," said interim-chairman Joe Gatt in Kinshasa.
Majority-owned by American company AT&T, Telecel runs Zaire's only workable telephone system, on which Zaire's politicians, business men and even the military rely for communications.
(Corrects from "Majority-owned by America's AT&T..." to make clear company is American but not state-owned.)

A Reuters correspondent in Bukavu, eastern Zaire, this week saw a Tutsi man lying face down in a military cell beaten close to death. Nearby an old Tutsi man sat in a blood spattered tunic, his head in his hands.
Bukavu inhabitants said many Tutsis were killed by roving local militias and Rwandan Hutu hardliners. Zairean soldiers dumped some over the Rwandan border for protection.

Although some ancestors of Zaire's Tutsis came to the country over 200 years ago most arrived from Rwanda in the 1920s under Belgian colonial rule and settled around Masisi and Rutshuru in North Kivu district. Others came to find work in the 1950s, while still more fled ethnic war in Rwanda in 1959.
A seperate group of Tutsis calling themselves Banyamulenge, a community of about 300,000 who form the bulk of the rebels, settled in South Kivu district.
Prime Minister Kengo, himself half-Tutsi, on Thursday accused Uganda as well as the Tutsi-dominated armies of Rwanda and Burundi of invading Zaire.
But anti-Tutsi feeling is running deep. "We should chase out the enemy within," cigarette seller Baudoin Kabeya said in Kinshasa. "Kengo should go too, even his mother is Rwandan."
